title: OSHA Emergency Exit Checklist (29 CFR 1910.36)
subtitle: Use on routine walk-throughs of exit routes and after changes to layout, storage or doors.
instructions: Mark every item OK, Defect or N/A, and note which exit route and door each mark refers to.
Record each Defect with its location, report it to the person responsible for the building, and recheck the item once it is corrected.
Site rules, local fire codes and door or hardware manufacturers' instructions may add checks.

sections.title: Exit doors and locking
items: Each exit route door opens from inside by hand, with no key, tool or special knowledge needed.
Any locking device on an exit discharge door, such as a panic bar, locks only from the outside.
Devices and alarms on exit doors
No device or alarm is fitted that would stop the door being used in an emergency if the device or alarm failed.
Each door connecting a room to an exit route is side-hinged.
Doors from rooms designed for more than 50 people, or from high hazard areas, swing outward toward the exit.
Fire doors on openings into exits
Each opening into an exit has a self-closing fire door that is shut, or closes automatically when the fire or employee alarm sounds.
Fire door, frame and hardware are listed or approved by an NRTL.

sections.title: Width, height and obstructions
items: Exit access measures 28 inches (71.1 cm) or more at every point along the route.
No stored goods, racking, equipment or furniture sticks out into the route far enough to cut its width under the minimum.
Ceiling along the route is seven feet six inches (2.3 m) or higher.
No light, duct, pipe or other projection hangs lower than six feet eight inches (2.0 m) above the floor.
Exit and discharge width after a single access
Where one exit access feeds an exit or discharge, the exit and discharge are at least as wide as that access.
The route does not narrow or lose capacity anywhere between the work area and the exit discharge.

sections.title: Number of routes and exit discharge
items: At least two exit routes are available, unless a single route has been assessed as allowing all employees to evacuate safely.
Exit routes are as far apart as practical, so fire or smoke blocking one leaves the other usable.
Each exit route is a permanent part of the workplace.
Each exit discharge leads directly outside or to a street, walkway, refuge area, public way or open space with outside access.
The area at the end of the discharge is large enough for the occupants likely to use that route.
Exit stairs that continue beyond the discharge level are interrupted there by a door, partition or other means that clearly shows the way out.

sections.title: Outdoor exit routes
items: Outdoor route meets the same minimum height and width as an indoor exit route.
Guardrails protect unenclosed sides wherever a fall hazard exists.
Route is covered where snow or ice is likely to build up, or accumulation is removed before it becomes a slipping hazard.
Route is reasonably straight, with smooth, solid, substantially level walkways.
No dead-end on the route is longer than 20 feet (6.2 m).

references: 29 CFR 1910.36: Design and construction requirements for exit routes (Part 1910 Subpart E: Exit Routes and Emergency Planning)
Source: eCFR, Title 29, text as of 2026-11-09
